Pfizer also Tuesday announced that Cecile Guegan , who has held various finance leadership roles at the company over the last two decades, stepped in as chief financial officer this month. She had served as interim CFO since August, when Pfizer's former CFO, Dave Denton, stepped down to take the same position at Nike. The company is now expecting full-year revenue to total $62 billion to $64 billion, which compares with a previous outlook of $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion. The low end of that sales range would be roughly flat or down slightly compared with 2025 revenue of $62.6 billion. Still, Pfizer cited its "strong year-to-date performance" as a driver for the guidance hike. The pharmaceutical giant now expects full-year adjusted profit of between $2.95 and $3.05 per share. That compares with previous guidance of between $2.80 and $3 per share. Smith Collection | Archive Photos | Getty Images That includes a one-time $650 million charge, or a negative impact of 10 cents per share, recorded in the third quarter tied to the company's licensing and collaboration agreement with Chinese cancer drugmaker Innovent Biologics. Pfizer is working on a comeback story after its massive pandemic-era success waned. As demand for Covid products drops and generic rivals threaten its biggest moneymakers, CEO Albert Bourla is looking to jump-start growth through strategic acquisitions, fresh cancer drugs and a big bet on weight loss treatments through its acquisition of Metsera. Pfizer in August expanded its multiyear cost-cutting efforts to help offset sharp declines in Covid product sales, and is now targeting roughly $9.7 billion in net savings through 2029. Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 87 cents adjusted vs. 73 cents expected Revenue: $16.58 billion vs. $15.87 billion expected Pfizer reported third-quarter revenue of $16.58 billion, relatively flat from the same period a year ago. The company cited an operational decrease of $57 million, primarily due to lower Covid revenues, and a $15 million negative impact from foreign exchange. That was offset by strong sales of key products like its blood thinner Eliquis and targeted cancer drug Padcev, which jumped and beat expectations. Eliquis in particular raked in $2.52 billion in sales, up 25%. Analysts were expecting revenue of $2.40 billion, according to StreetAccount. Padcev posted $720 million in revenue for the period, which compares with the $658 million that analysts were expecting. Sales of Pfizer's newly launched and acquired products grew 32% operationally. That includes Padcev, its respiratory syncytial virus vaccine Abrysvo, its pneumococcal shot Prevnar 20 and oral lung cancer drug Lorbrena, among several other products. Pfizer's Covid products also topped estimates for the quarter despite seeing steep sales declines. The company's Covid vaccine generated $808 million in sales, which compares with the $770.4 million that analysts were expecting, StreetAccount estimates show. Meanwhile, Pfizer's antiviral pill, Paxlovid, booked $449 million in sales, coming in above the $394.1 million that analysts were expecting. The company booked net income of $3.24 billion, or 56 cents per share, for the period. That compares with net income of $3.54 billion, or 62 cents per share, during the third quarter of 2025. Excluding certain items, including restructuring charges and costs associated with intangible assets, Pfizer posted earnings per share of 87 cents for the quarter. Icon Sportswire | Icon Sportswire | Getty Images When a CEO talks politics, people tend to get nervous — especially when the issues don't seem to directly affect the company. Yet "some fundamental issues" call for a public stance, even if the subject doesn't obviously or immediately affect a CEO's company, former American Express CEO Ken Chenault told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday. Any threat to democratic institutions or processes in the U.S. can ultimately sow political and economic instability that could have a negative impact on any business, regardless of the sector or industry, he added. "If you want to build an enduring company, you should care about what happens in our society," said Chenault, who stepped down as American Express CEO in 2018 after 37 years at the financial services giant, including nearly 17 as chief executive. He currently serves as chairman and managing director of venture capital firm General Catalyst. CEOs shouldn't speak out on every political matter, Chenault said. But those seeking lasting success need "long-term perspective" about any risks and opportunities that could ultimately affect their companies, he suggested. Business leaders often refrain from speaking out on political issues for fear of alienating customers or their own employees . Some companies have found success weaving politics into their public image — outdoor apparel company Patagonia is among the best known — but taking a publicly political stance is most often met with mixed opinions, according to a 2025 study from a group of Ivy League researchers. On the whole, the average person generally prefers CEOs to stay silent on divisive political issues, the study found. Yet with American voters heading to the polls on Tuesday, Chenault specifically pointed to the issue of voting rights as one that corporate leaders like himself should publicly acknowledge. As the Republican Party braces to potentially lose national and state-level seats in the midterm elections , President Donald Trump has declined to say he would unconditionally accept the electoral results. Instead, the president has promised to accept the results "if they're honest elections," The Washington Post reported on Oct. 27. "If, in fact, the upcoming election is threatened and the verdict of the election is not accepted, that is not an issue that I would be quiet [on]," Chenault said, adding: "Nothing is more fundamental than preserving and strengthening our democracy [and] the fundamental right to vote." Political instability can hurt a country's economy, research suggests . One potential path for democratic erosion to harm business: A breakdown of the rule of law can scare off investors looking to deploy capital or build new companies, Princeton University political scientist Layna Mosley found in a July 2023 report published by nonpartisan organizations The Brookings Institution and States United Democracy Center. As American Express CEO, Chenault weighed in publicly on some political issues that did have an immediate impact on his company. One of his more prominent stances was an acknowledgment of the financial industry's need to adapt and accept additional regulatory oversight following the 2008 financial crisis, for example. More recently, Chenault has spoken somewhat frequently about the importance of robust voting rights. In March 2021, he and former Merck CEO Ken Frazier called on corporate leaders to push back on political efforts to restrict voting access in the U.S. In particular, Chenault — one of the first few Black CEOs of a Fortune 500 company, upon his appointment at American Express in 2001 — spoke out against policies that voting rights groups have criticized as disproportionately disenfranchising voters of color. "Corporations have to stand up. There is no middle ground," Chenault told "Squawk Box" on March 31, 2021. "This is about all Americans having the right to vote, but we need to recognize the special history of the denial of the right to vote for Black Americans, and we will not be silent." Meta previously raised $25 billion in an April bond sale, and said last week that it plans to raise $95 billion in an effort to fund its AI initiatives. Stocks making the biggest moves midday: Apple, Palantir, Nvidia, Coinbase, Bloom Energy & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: AAPL, PLTR, NVDA, COIN, BE Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. Coinbase — The cryptocurrency exchange's stock rallied 8% Tuesday after sliding 15% in the three trading days through Monday. Coinbase reported third-quarter results postmarket last Thursday showing weaker crypto trading volumes, leading Morgan Stanley to lower its rating to underweight and slash its price target by 53% Monday. Shopify — The e-commerce platform's stock fell more than 5% Tuesday after the company missed estimates on subscription gross profit and gross merchandise volume. Overall, quarterly revenue came in at $3.74 billion, just below LSEG estimates of $3.75 billion. Shopify said it sees revenue growth in the "low thirties" range year over year for the fourth quarter, versus LSEG estimates of 32.1%. Shopify expects free cash flow margin to be consistent with the fourth quarter of 2025 . Bloom Energy — The maker of solid oxide fuel cells saw shares gain nearly 10% after Barclays upgraded Bloom to overweight from equal weight on Tuesday. The bank cited higher-than-expected demand, but lowered its 12-month price target to $289 from $319, which still implies upside of about 47% from Monday's close. Thomson Reuters — Shares slipped 7.5% after Thomson reported weaker-than-expected earnings. In the third quarter, the content and technology provider delivered adjusted earnings of 81 cents compared with 83 cents that analysts polled by FactSet had estimated. Revenue was in line with estimates at $1.83 billion. ON Semiconductor — Shares advanced 4% after ON posted third-quarter results that topped estimates. Adjusted earnings for the period totaled 90 cents per share on revenue of $1.72 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG estimated 88 cents a share on $1.70 billion. DuPont de Nemours — Shares climbed about 9% after the giant chemical company reported third-quarter financial results . DuPont posted adjusted earnings of $2.09 on revenue of $1.87 billion, versus the FactSet consensus estimate of $1.87 per share on $1.84 billion. DuPont raised the full-year financial outlook and expects organic growth to be about 4.5%. Fiserv — The financial services and fintech company's stock gained 12% after third-quarter earnings surpassed estimates. Fiserv earned an adjusted $1.75 per share against the FactSet consensus estimate of $1.72. Fiserv also expects to repurchase $500 million of common stock in the fourth quarter under its existing buyback authorization. Artificial intelligence plays — A slate of stocks tied to the AI trade perked up after several days of hard selling. The iShares AI Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) jumped 2%, while shares of chipmakers Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices bounced 3% and 5%, respectively. Shares of memory stock Sandisk advanced almost 4%, and shares of neocloud names Nebius and Ire gained 7% and 9%, respectively. Revvity — Shares gained 11% after the life sciences company raised full-year pro forma adjusted earnings per share guidance to $5.40 to $5.45 from a previous range of $5.30 to $5.40. Pfizer — The pharma giant's stock eased 1% after reporting third-quarter results. Pfizer earned 87 cents per share, excluding one-time items, on revenue of $16.58 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG estimated a profit of 73 cents per share on revenue of $15.87 billion. Zebra Technologies — The maker of barcode scanners and mobile computers used in retail and other industries saw shares fall 6% after third-quarter adjusted gross margin came in at 46%. The FactSet consensus estimate was for 47.7%. Top- and bottom-line results for the period beat expectations. Gartner — Shares slid 13% despite third-quarter results beating expectations. Gartner also issued better-than-expected adjusted earnings and revenue guidance for the full year. Palantir Technologies — Palantir shares fell 2% despite the company's third-quarter adjusted earnings topping Wall Street's estimates. The company's U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, topping U.S. government revenue of $953 million. Palantir also projected about $2.65 billion in fourth-quarter revenue and $8.53 billion for all of 2026. Apple — Apple shares weakened 2% after the iPhone maker reported a disappointing margin forecast , and as iPad sales in the fiscal fourth quarter missed the Street's estimates. — CNBC's Deena Zaidi, Scott Schnipper, Davis Giangiulio, Darla Mercado and Fred Imbert contributed reporting.

headlines.article_text: Palantir stock falls despite Q3 earnings beat Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Palantir shares fell on Tuesday after the software company reported Q3 earnings. The software company saw a slowdown in U.S. commercial total contract value growth. Apple shares also sank as the company reckons with a global memory crunch and a scramble for computer components. In this article AAPL PLTR Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:00 02:00 Palantir's CEO on Q3 results and boom in company's commercial business Morning Call Palantir shares fell on Tuesday after the software company reported third-quarter earnings and analysts pointed to signs of a slowdown in total contract value and other "forward indicators." U.S. commercial revenue topped government for the first time, but the company closed $1.5 billion in TCV in the segment, up 11% from last year. In Q2, Palantir closed a record $2.1 billion worth of TCV in the segment, which was up 153% from the prior year. Investors will "no doubt be looking for evidence in subsequent quarters that 11% growth in U.S. commercial TCV bookings is a fluke of duration and not something structural," a Piper Sandler note from Monday said. "We believe that is the case and demand for PLTR's solutions still very much outstrip supply." In a Tuesday note, Goldman Sachs analysts noted that the company attributed some of this to shorter contract durations. "The key will be converting shorter duration contracts into longer duration commitments, which Palantir has done successfully in the past," the analysts wrote. Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time, Palantir said in its earnings report. Palantir stock chart. Apple's earnings The iPhone maker reported better-than-expected revenue in its fourth-quarter earnings, but fell short of estimates on iPad sales and issued a margin forecast that disappointed investors. Apple 's statement marked the first earnings report since John Ternus took over as CEO from Tim Cook in September. The stock fell more than 2% on Tuesday. The company is reckoning with a global memory crunch and a scramble for computer components. Memory costs were higher this quarter than in the June period, the company said Monday. Despite the price surge, Ternus said Apple had just capped off its "best fiscal year ever." He told CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos that Apple's growth came despite supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds. "The concern is profitability," said Violeta Todorova, senior research analyst at Leverage Shares. "Management pointed to memory as the main pressure, together with the cost of rolling out Siri AI. Memory shortages are also expected to limit Mac and iPad supply, as demand has run ahead of plans." Apple shares have risen 25% in 2026, ahead of other big tech names, but that premium leaves "little room for disappointment," Todorova added.
